tool.excerpt: Hawaii's 550-Year-Old Hōlei Sea Arch Collapses Into Pacific Ocean, 90-Foot Landmark Leaves Internet Heartbroken Free Press Journal e-Paper Get App Home Mumbai News FPJ Shorts Entertainment Bollywood Hollywood Television Regional Film News Movie Reviews Business Technology Games Features Weekend Lifestyle India Sports SportVot Viral Education Study Abroad Tech --> Home Lifestyle Hawaii's 550-Year-Old Hōlei Sea Arch Collapses Into Pacific Ocean, 90-Foot Landmark Leaves Internet Heartbroken Hawaii's 550-Year-Old Hōlei Sea Arch Collapses Into Pacific Ocean, 90-Foot Landmark Leaves Internet Heartbroken Hawaii’s 550-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot lava-rock formation at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean. The arch was still visible on September 23 but had disappeared by September 27, with no witnesses to the collapse. The National Park Service said coastal instability and earlier volcanic activity had affected the surrounding cliffs for years. Aanchal C Updated: Saturday, October 03, 2026, 12:26 PM IST Hōlei Sea Arch collapses into the Pacific Ocean. | Image Courtesy: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park Some landmarks seem permanent simply because they have been around for generations. But nature has its own timeline. Hawaii’s Hōlei Sea Arch, a towering lava-rock formation that had stood along the coastline for roughly 550 years, has now disappeared into the Pacific Ocean. The dramatic natural landmark, which rose around 90 feet (27.4 metres) above the coastline, was one of the most photographed formations in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park. Its sudden disappearance has left visitors and social media users reflecting on how quickly even centuries-old natural wonders can change. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Hawaii Volcanoes National Park (@hawaiivolcanoesnps) Hōlei Sea Arch collapses The National Park Service (NPS) confirmed on Wednesday, September 30, that the Hōlei Sea Arch had collapsed. The structure was still visible from the coast on September 23, but by the night of September 27, it was gone. No one witnessed the collapse, so its exact timing remains unknown. According to the park service, the arch may have fallen while the area was closed during Tropical Storm Nolo over the weekend. Read Also No Long Weekends In 2027?
